Although multi-source detection models have been proposed to mitigate this, they frequently fail to generalize across domains because they rely on source-specific linguistic and semantic features. Furthermore, existing cross-domain models for fake news detection lack the ability to leverage structural information from co-occurrence graphs. To address these limitations, we introduce Optimal-Structure-Transfer, a method that transfers structural features between domains while optimizing for the target domain. By integrating this approach with a state-of-the-art cross-domain detection model, our method achieves superior performance. Experiments on datasets from both social media and professional news platforms demonstrate that our approach effectively overcomes the limitations of current multi-source, cross-domain fake news detection methods. Additionally, our model generalizes well to unseen events, as shown by results from a dynamic test dataset. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/haomingchen/OST.

Laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) represents a minimally invasive technique for ablating intracranial lesions through direct thermal destruction. This study introduces an automated, intracranial temperature mapping system that utilizes magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to guide LITT procedures. The primary objective of this work is to evaluate the accuracy of a novel, physics-informed deep learning model for reconstructing 3D temperature distributions from sparse sensor data during intracranial ablations. This reconstruction algorithm integrates a convolutional neural network (CNN) with physical constraints derived from a biologically realistic heat diffusion model. Using a dataset of 200 real-time MRI thermometry (RTT) recordings from six sheep, the model was trained on a sparse subset and subsequently tested on both unseen data and the original dataset to assess reconstruction fidelity. Results indicate that the hybrid CNN model achieves high accuracy in reconstructing 3D temperature fields from 2D cross-sectional RTT measurements, with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.81 °C across the entire volume and 0.64 °C within the ablation zone. These findings suggest that this approach offers a promising solution for enabling real-time, three-dimensional temperature monitoring in sparse-field intracranial thermal ablations, thereby supporting the precise delivery of LITT. Furthermore, the methodology presented here can be adapted for other types of thermal ablative therapies.

Feature extraction serves as an effective strategy for mitigating dimensionality challenges inherent in high-dimensional datasets. Given the recent surge in interest toward self-supervised learning due to its capacity to harness vast unlabeled data, this study investigates a contrastive learning framework grounded in positive and negative pair concepts. Drawing from recent advances in feature extraction via graph neural networks (GNNs), we introduce a contrastive GNN framework designed to learn robust embeddings through the integration of graph structures and contrastive principles. Specifically, we define a graph-based supervision mechanism and two distinct contrastive learning strategies: a "pair-based" approach and a "graph-based" approach. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method for selecting optimal embeddings without relying on manual feature supervision. Our experimental results, derived from both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrate that our framework effectively leverages structural information to produce superior embeddings compared to existing methods. These findings indicate that the contrastive learning concept—when applied to structural data through a combination of positive and negative pairs—yields performance comparable to supervised learning. To facilitate further research, our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/PhucNguyen1996/SSL-HD. Although large language models (LLMs) achieve human-level performance across many natural language tasks, their reliance on textual descriptions of structured knowledge—such as knowledge graphs (KGs)—limits the efficiency of learning and infusing new knowledge. This paper reviews recent advances in embedding knowledge graphs into LLMs, covering the creation of knowledge graph embeddings, training-based methods, and prompt-based techniques. We also examine recent research on multimodal knowledge graphs and offer recommendations for future directions. This study investigates the connection between the shadow radius and temperature to explore thermodynamic phase transitions of charged AdS black holes within the presence of non-linear electrodynamics. The shadow radius is modeled using a power-law formulation that incorporates charge and non-linear electrodynamics parameters, while temperature is defined via the extended Hilbert hotel criterion. Consequently, both the shadow radius and temperature are expressed as functions of the horizon radius. Analyzing the relationship between these two variables reveals that the coexistence of non-linear electrodynamics and AdS curvature causes the shadow radius to exhibit non-monotonic behavior with respect to temperature. Furthermore, the (shadow radius, temperature) plane is divided into distinct regions representing different physical phases, with phase transition points identified through the (shadow radius, temperature) curve and the ($r_h$, T) curve. Additionally, the (shadow radius, entropy) curve offers insights into underlying microscopic mechanisms. Finally, the influence of mass, AdS curvature, and non-linear electrodynamics on the shadow radius, temperature, and phase transitions is examined. Ultimately, the findings indicate that altering the AdS curvature or the non-linear electrodynamics parameter significantly impacts the shadow radius, temperature, and associated phase transitions. These results suggest that the shadow radius serves as an effective probe for uncovering hidden characteristics of black holes. Regarding future research directions, exploring the impact of other modified gravity models on the shadow radius and temperature could be a promising avenue. Such an analysis would help clarify whether this phenomenon is specific to AdS black holes under non-linear electrodynamics or applicable more broadly. Moreover, further examining the image size observed by distant astronomers under varying non-linear electrodynamics conditions would be valuable. Ultimately, this work underscores the shadow radius's utility as a crucial tool for uncovering the microscopic mechanisms of black holes.

Reconstructing quantum states in continuous-variable systems, such as the radiation field, is complicated by the infinite-dimensional nature of the underlying Hilbert space. While numerous reconstruction methods exist, they often demand a vast number of experimental runs to gather the required data. Recently, quantum state reconstruction via optical tomograms was demonstrated theoretically, and recently, this approach was applied experimentally to generate the Wigner function for simple Gaussian states using a single- and double-heterodyne measurement scheme. Although the extraction of the Wigner function from the optical tomogram relies on a linear integral transformation, determining this transformation for general states has remained challenging. In this work, we present a straightforward method to derive the Star-product from the optical tomogram, which is implemented simply through discrete processing of the data. Furthermore, we propose an efficient algorithm to calculate the Wigner function from the optical tomogram without relying on the intermediate steps of the Star-product or Fourier transformation. To validate this new method, we first verify it for Gaussian states and then perform single-mode and two-mode Wigner reconstruction for non-Gaussian squeezed-cat states. Additionally, we investigate the transition from quantum to classical behavior in a Schrödinger-cat state through its optical tomogram, Wigner function, and trace distance. Our proposed method for Wigner reconstruction is straightforward and requires no additional experimental setup; it only demands simple data processing. This approach can be easily adapted to extract the Wavefunction, Husimi-Q function, and other representations from the optical tomogram. Finally, this method offers a practical solution for measuring the Wigner function in multi-mode systems where other approaches become computationally challenging. Our findings provide a new pathway for extracting the Wigner function from optical experimental data and may find applications in various areas of quantum physics. Our work demonstrates that the optical tomogram serves as a fundamental quantity from which all other quantum descriptors can be derived. Specifically, we establish a direct linear relationship between the optical tomogram and the Wigner function, and subsequently between the Wigner function and other representations like the Wavefunction and Husimi-Q function. Consequently, the optical tomogram can be regarded as a primary descriptor for characterizing the radiation field's state. Finally, our proposed method for deriving the Wigner function from the optical tomogram for multi-mode fields represents a significant advancement, particularly for high-pixel-count scenarios in quantum imaging. In summary, our findings offer a simple, practical method for Wigner state reconstruction in quantum optics and related fields, potentially enabling new discoveries in quantum imaging and other areas of physics. Generally, constructing the submodule lattice $L(M)$ for a specific module $M$ presents significant challenges. For certain classes of modules, explicit constructions of $L(M)$ have been achieved by defining join irreducible submodules and organizing them into a candidate structure, which is then verified to constitute the complete lattice of submodules. This article extends such a construction to $\Z_{p^2}$-modules, where $p$ is a prime, by offering a comprehensive characterization of their join irreducible submodules. Additionally, we establish a detailed structure for this class of modules and provide a Hasse diagram illustrating all its components. Finally, we apply these findings to determine the distributive lattices of rank two and three. Our analysis reveals that every semi-simple module $M$ over $\Z_{p^2}$, with $p$ a prime, yields a submodule lattice $L(M)$ that corresponds either to the simple lattice $J_3$ or, when $M$ is a direct sum of two non-isomorphic simple modules, to either $J_2\times J_2$ or $D_3$. We conclude by outlining open challenges regarding the distribution of $L(M)$ for modules defined over more general Artinian local rings. These distributions form a subset of the Ames-Dubuc-Solberg taxonomy of lattices of composite type. Our detailed examination of $M$ as a $\Z_{p^2}$-module also enables us to explicitly calculate the Hamming distance between any two submodules of $M$.

This study demonstrates that certain well-established recurrent operators—specifically the recurrent curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators—play a crucial role in determining whether biharmonic hypersurfaces are minimal within Euclidean space. Additionally, the paper identifies new recurrent curvature operators and introduces a class of hypersurfaces characterized by a combination of a recurrent curvature operator, a recurrent shape operator, and a recurrent Wirtinger operator. For these newly defined combinations, the authors determine their explicit forms and examine the nature of the corresponding biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean environment. Ultimately, it is concluded that for some of these configurations, multiple distinct geometrical structures coexist. The significance of these findings lies in their potential to advance the understanding of the geometry of hypersurfaces in Euclidean space and related manifolds. Furthermore, these results suggest promising directions for future research, particularly regarding the investigation of other recurrent operators and variational problems associated with mappings between manifolds. For any rational number $p/q$, numeration in base $p/q$ generally yields an infinite sequence of integers representing the value of each prefix when evaluated to a nonnegative integer. We examine the syntactic homomorphism $\eta_{p/q}$, which maps the set of words with a nonnegative trace in base $p/q}$ to $\mathbb{N}_0$ and assigns $-1$ to the remainder words. It is established that $\eta_{p/q}$ constitutes a regular homomorphism. Focusing on regular subsets of words whose $\eta_{p/q}$ image is finite, we identify the syntactic monoids of these subsets and characterize those subsets that form languages recognized by a specific monoid. In particular, we prove that the prefix set of a rational regular word is a $p/q$-regular word, and we provide a constructive method to determine the regular expression of the set of words with even values in base $p/q}$. Finally, we offer a constructive approach to construct the regular tree automaton corresponding to the commutant of a $p/q$-regular set of words. As an application, we present a simple algorithm to decide whether the Diophantine equation $f(n)=m$, where $f(n)$ is a $p/q$-regular integer polynomial and $n, m \in \mathbb{Z}$, is recognizable; that is, we can construct the regular expression for the subset of $\mathbb{N}$ satisfying this equation. Our constructions are explicit and can be executed on a Turing machine. Additionally, we detail the syntactic monoids for several concrete examples of $p/q$-regular sets of words. Finally, we outline open questions regarding the regularity of other Diophantine sets related to $p/q$-regular sets of words and integer or $p/q$-rationally regular sequences.

In the early 1930s, K. Menger explored the concept of dimension, proposing a general definition suitable for metric and semi-metric spaces that extended Brouwer's existing theory for metric spaces. However, this work remained largely unnoticed until the 1960s, when P. Nyikos and W. Gaschutz independently rediscovered and generalized it within the context of linear spaces and vector spaces. This paper aims to further generalize the definition of $n$-dimensionality to cover a broader class of structured sets. Additionally, we investigate the uniqueness of this generalization and analyze its fundamental properties. Finally, we define a notion of dimension for arbitrary structured sets and examine how this concept applies to specific set types. Our results demonstrate that unique generalizations of this concept exist for several important structured sets, including topological spaces, proximity spaces, uniform spaces, and various types of convergence spaces. Furthermore, we establish uniqueness for topological groups, nearness spaces, and Riemannian manifolds, while also introducing a new concept of dimension for nearness spaces.

Neural network-based point cloud models have achieved significant success in tasks like recognition, classification, and segmentation. However, these models remain susceptible to adversarial attacks, which can deceive models through subtle modifications. Unlike image data, point clouds lack a fixed shape and orientation, enabling more complex transformations beyond simple shifts and rotations. This paper introduces a unified framework for point cloud models that categorizes common 3D transformations into three groups: invariant transformations (such as shifts and rotations), semi-invariant transformations (like scaling and shearing), and non-invariant transformations (including perspective and fisheye effects). We systematically analyzed how these transformations impact model accuracy and defined a hierarchy of transformations based on their impact. Furthermore, we developed an algorithm to identify unknown transformations and demonstrated its effectiveness against various common and rare distortions. Finally, we proposed an ensemble defense strategy against arbitrary transformations, which outperformed existing methods in both accuracy and robustness. This chapter serves as an introduction to formal methods applicable to program verification, offering a concise overview without exhaustive detail. It begins by defining the concept of correctness and outlining a verification workflow. The discussion then covers various specifications for correctness, including Hoare triples, refinement types, and testing. Fiber-reinforced composites featuring nanofiller-modified polymer matrices hold significant promise for enhancing the safety of high-risk engineering structures. These materials possess an inherent self-sensing capability, as their electrical conductivity alters in response to deformation and damage. This phenomenon, termed piezoresistivity, has been widely utilized for damage detection through electrical resistance measurements and tomographic imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). While these approaches are effective at identifying the existence of damage, they fall short in determining its specific characteristics, such as whether a crack is open or closed. This paper introduces a novel method for characterizing damage in piezoresistive composites by integrating optical coherence tomography (OCT) with electrical conductivity maps. The OCT captures detailed structural information about the damage, which is then converted into a dielectric contrast image using a finite element method (FEM) model to simulate conductivity variations. This hybrid strategy was applied to identify and characterize cracks within a unidirectional (UD) carbon fiber/Elastomer-Black Diamond (CB75) composite containing 0.75 wt% nanofiller. The results demonstrate that the OCT-FEM approach yields accurate damage characterizations that align well with direct visual observations from digital images. Furthermore, this method offers distinct advantages over EIT, particularly regarding the precise localization of small damages.

We introduce a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces that prioritizes geometric and algebraic foundations, minimizing reliance on calculus. This approach enables the development of a vector calculus suitable for elementary physics courses, offering an alternative to the traditional tensor analysis found in general relativity. By reformulating standard tensor analysis on pseudo-Euclidean spaces (of signature $(3,1)$), we can extend this vector calculus to those spaces. This extension allows for the construction of an electromagnetic theory in pseudo-Euclidean spaces that aligns with our Euclidean-based electromagnetic theory. Furthermore, we can define special relativistic and general relativistic physics on pseudo-Euclidean spaces without altering their underlying mathematical structure. Our analysis of Euclidean and pseudo-Euclidean spaces mirrors the treatment of vector, complex, and Hilbert spaces in quantum mechanics. Consequently, our work suggests that Euclidean and pseudo-Euclidean spaces, rather than general Riemannian or pseudo-Riemannian manifolds, serve as the appropriate mathematical foundation for quantum mechanics and general relativity. To facilitate this research, we have created an accompanying computer algebra system, Tensoriax, available at http://vixar.org/Tensoriax/. This system has been utilized to verify many of the calculations presented herein.

Advancements in technology have enabled the rapid growth of massive MIMO systems, which are essential for delivering high data rates and enhancing coverage in fifth-generation wireless networks. These systems often face significant challenges related to matrix inversion, a computationally intensive task. While classic direct iterative methods for matrix inversion suffer from slow convergence, recent advances in compressed sensing have introduced fast, non-iterative approaches that require a certain sparsity condition. This paper proposes a novel combination of an iterative algorithm and a random projection technique to create a new non-iterative method suitable for sparse massive MIMO matrix inversion. Numerical results confirm that this approach achieves high accuracy and converges rapidly, performing well even when the sparsity level is low. Additionally, the method remains effective across various pilot lengths and system dimensions. Finally, this new approach can be applied to optimize multiple access point deployments and improve massive MIMO beamforming and null-steering techniques. The proposed method is defined by the equation: "Iterative Matrix Inversion via Random Projection and Sparsity Exploitation".

Contextual linear bandits represent a theoretically significant model with extensive practical applications. In the distributed memoryless contextual linear bandit setting, the goal is to minimize regret over $T$ rounds without access to more than five decades fewer contexts ($5\text{d}$) per round than the total time horizon $T$, and lacking any other information about the contexts beyond their historical record. This work examines both stochastic and adversarial frameworks, establishing near-optimal regret bounds that match the current upper limits up to logarithmic factors for both scenarios. Specifically, we introduce an algorithm achieving an upper bound of $d \log(T)/\sqrt{\log(T_{\text{eff}})}$, where $d$ denotes the dimension of the context vector and $T_{\text{eff}}$ corresponds to the count of contexts encountered at least once. Our approach leverages a public-key encryption scheme to encode an estimate of the contexts' distribution, which is then utilized to construct an effective horizon. Numerical experiments conducted in a distributed environment demonstrate that our method outperforms existing baselines by a substantial margin, particularly when contexts follow a heavy-tailed distribution. These results indicate that sacrificing a polylogarithmic term in $T$ to utilize approximately $5\text{d}$ bits per context can yield significant performance gains in contexts with heavy tails. Furthermore, these findings suggest that similar strategies could be valuable for other problems where contexts exhibit heavy-tailed characteristics.

The vertical shear instability (VSI) is a hydrodynamical mechanism potentially responsible for generating turbulence in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks.
